title: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man? sun → moon → fire → speech → self (4.3)
hook: a king asks what light a person has, and takes the lights away one at a time
tomorrow: dreaming — the self creates its own world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the debate ended: Shakalya pushed as someone else's tool, and lost his head. Your line was don't ask past the limit. Did you trade a question to win for one to know? Day three hundred eighty-two.

The power goes out at night. The streetlights die, the screens go black, your phone is at one percent and then it's gone. You can't see your own hand. And then, from the next room, someone calls your name. You get up and walk toward the voice. Something very like that moment is in the Brihadaranyaka, in a conversation between a king and a sage with no crowd and no cows. Just King Janaka, asking one question and taking the lights away one by one.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T SEE YOUR HAND.` → `YOU WALK TOWARD THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: The debate is over. In book four, Yajnavalkya visits the king again, quietly. Yajnavalkya, Janaka asks, what light does a person have? The sun, your majesty. By the light of the sun a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. True. But when the sun has set, what light does a person have? The moon. And when the sun has set and the moon has set? Fire. And when the sun has set, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out? Speech. That's why, when you can't even see your own hand, wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. True, Yajnavalkya. And when the sun has set, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, and speech has fallen silent, what light does a person have then? And Yajnavalkya says: atmaivasya jyotir bhavati. The self is their light. By the light of the self a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. Which is the self? The one made of knowing, among the senses, the light within the heart. Look at how carefully the king builds it. Each light is real, and each one can go out. The sun sets. The moon sets. Fire dies. Even voices go quiet. The question is what's left when all of them are gone. Sit in a dark room with your eyes open: nothing to look at, and still something knows it's dark. That knowing, the text says, is the light that was there under all the others.
screen: `THE SUN, THE MOON, THE FIRE.` · `SPEECH: WE WALK TOWARD A VOICE.` · `THE SELF IS THEIR LIGHT.` · `THE LIGHT WITHIN THE HEART.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes taking the lights away. Sit, and close your eyes. The sun has set: notice there's still something seeing the dark behind your eyelids. The moon has set; the fire's out: still knowing. Now let the voices go quiet, the ones outside and the one in your head. Rest in whatever is still aware. You don't need to name it. Just notice it's been on this whole time. The bell holds the time.
Jyoti. Light. In Janaka's question, what a person has when the sun, the moon, the fire and every voice are gone: the self is their light.
Your line: your own light. Tonight, when you turn off the last light, pause in the dark for one breath and notice what's still awake. Day three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Hindus light lamps at dawn and dusk and at every festival, and the Brihadaranyaka's line that the self is a person's own light is often quoted by teachers when explaining the inner meaning of the lamp.

match.prompt: the lights, in order — tap the pairs.

myth: in Janaka's list, the last outer light is fire
after fire comes speech: in the dark, you go toward a voice.
Yajnavalkya calls the self the light within the heart
the one made of knowing, among the senses.
when every outer light is gone, the text says a person has no light

fork.setup: it's pitch dark. no sun, no moon, no fire. you can't see your own hand. how does the text say you find your way?
fork.reveal: wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. speech is a light too, until it falls silent and only the self is left.

original.note: Sanskrit jyotis: light. ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavati, the self is their light (4.3.6).

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle about the sun and the moon.
what it means: every outer light can go out; what is left, and was there all along, is the self.
what a scholar hears: kiṃjyotir ayaṃ puruṣa (4.3.2): the light-sequence leads to the self as 'the light within the heart' (hṛdy antarjyotiḥ, 4.3.7).

notes: 4.3.1 says Yajnavalkya came to Janaka intending not to speak, but Janaka had earlier been granted a boon to ask anything; this framing is omitted. Confirm whether it should be included.
The sequence of lights (4.3.2–6) is paraphrased; the speech line ('when one cannot see one's own hand, where a voice is raised, there one goes') follows 4.3.5 closely. Confirm.
Sanskrit transliterated without diacritics: ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavati.

Reviewer edit: the hook no longer says the dark-room moment is in the text 'nearly word for word' (only the walking-toward-a-voice line, 4.3.5, is close). The teach no longer says book four 'opens' with this scene: 4.1–4.2 (Yajnavalkya and Janaka on six partial definitions of Brahman, and the self as neti neti) come first; 4.3 is a later visit.
